newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Minister backs slower sales of Australia wool.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Minister backs slower sales of Australia wool.

text.p: Australian Primary Industries Minister John Anderson said on Friday he would recommend slower disposal of the country's wool stockpile from mid 1997.

Under Anderson's plan, to be taken to cabinet, the minimum rate of disposal would fall to 135,000 bales per quarter from January, compared with current sales of 182,000 to 192,000 per quarter. From July, the minimum rate of disposal would fall to 90,000 per quarter, Anderson said in a statement.
From January, a 350,000-bales-per-quarter upper limit would apply to sales from the stockpile, which was accumulated in the late 1980s and early 1990s as a result of a failed price-support scheme.

"The priority now is for the industry to manage the transition of the market to a situation in a few years time when the stockpile has little, if any, influence on the market," Anderson said, announcing his plan after a meeting with industry leaders.
"The new selling rules for Wool International (the stockpile manager) will allow lower sales when the market is depressed."
Overall, Anderson's plan would see the stockpile sold more slowly, with a new deadline for disposal of December 2000 instead of September 1999.
The debt accumulated by the price-support scheme would be paid off by the end of 1998, the minister said.
The stockpile, which peaked at 4.7 million bales in the early 1990s, now stands at 2.13 million and Wool International's debt is just under A$1 billion.
Higher sales would occur as the market recovered, as confidently predicted, over the next two years, Anderson said.

WI's charter would include a requirement that its sales objective was to maximise the net return to the Australian wool growing industry, subject to the upper and lower sales limits and the target debt retirement date, he said.

The roundtable meeting between Anderson and industry representatives also agreed on the need to consider additional funding for promotion from WI's resources, or a higher promotion levy or a broader levy such as one on exports, he said.
The Wool Council of Australia, representing growers, would investigate possibilities, he said.
Anderson hailed Friday's roundtable as an "historic occasion" which agreed on more scope for commercial flexibility than possible under the stockpile fixed release schedule, in place since 1994.
Wool growers have long complained that the fixed release schedule depressed prices further during times of market weakness and wanted WI to have the flexibility to reduce its offerings at such times.
